curriculum.lesson_evidence: Audience knowledge is only the facts watchers already have. A stimulus is the starting idea you agree to build from, and this unit's stimulus is original: a lost house key. Riley was carrying the spare key so a younger sibling could get inside after school. After the last bell the key is not in Riley's hand. Alex, a friend, is there too. A given fact belongs on the opening list when the audience can already tell it, such as the school gate, the missing key, and the sibling who is waiting. A mystery is a fact you are saving. Where the key is must stay off the list, because the makers know more than the audience. Write the list in two columns: already known, and still hidden. That page is the evidence. Performing the moment is optional, needs everyone's consent, and needs an adult nearby.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
After the last bell, the group is listing audience knowledge for the lost house key. Which item must stay off that opening list?

FEEDBACK
Keep the school, the missing key, and the sibling, and leave the hiding place off. The gate, the empty hand, and the reason today matters are given facts the audience can already use. Naming the hiding place would hand them the mystery before the scene has earned it. If a fact needs a later action to be seen, it belongs in the hidden column.

WATCH FOR
Writers often add the hiding place because the makers already know it. The audience did not see you plan the scene. They only know what the opening shows or tells. Repair the list by moving any unshown location into the mystery column. Knowing the answer yourself is not the same as the audience knowing it.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
List what an audience already knows about a forgotten permission slip. The slip was due at the office before home time, and it is not in the student's folder. Write three given facts and one mystery that must stay off the opening list. Do not reuse the house key. A written list is the evidence. Acting is optional, with consent and an adult nearby.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teaching.misconception: Writing only a final praise word without naming a choice does not show arts thinking.
teaching.model: Riley's list names the school gate, the missing spare key, and a waiting sibling. Already known: they are at school after the bell; the spare house key is not in Riley's hand; someone at home needs that key today. Still hidden: the place the key fell, and whether the office can help. A second pass checks the list. 'Riley looks worried' can stay, because the face can show it. 'The key is under a bench' cannot stay, because nothing on stage has shown that yet. The audience meets the problem. They do not receive the answer. Look at each line, sound, movement or role choice that carries the idea.
teaching.rule: Make the arts idea visible: name the element, technique or performance choice you used and say what effect it creates.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

teaching.feedback: Keep the school, the missing key, and the sibling, and leave the hiding place off. The gate, the empty hand, and the reason today matters are given facts the audience can already use. Naming the hiding place would hand them the mystery before the scene has earned it. If a fact needs a later action to be seen, it belongs in the hidden column.

Knowing the answer yourself is not the same as the audience knowing it.

teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new artwork or performance.
teaching.model: Audience knowledge is only the facts watchers already have. A stimulus is the starting idea you agree to build from, and this unit's stimulus is original: a lost house key. Riley was carrying the spare key so a younger sibling could get inside after school. After the last bell the key is not in Riley's hand. Alex, a friend, is there too. A given fact belongs on the opening list when the audience can already tell it, such as the school gate, the missing key, and the sibling who is waiting. A mystery is a fact you are saving. Where the key is must stay off the list, because the makers know more than the audience. Write the list in two columns: already known, and still hidden. That page is the evidence. Performing the moment is optional, needs everyone's consent, and needs an adult nearby. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
